grants.title: CSIR Network Projects (NIH-CSIR Bilateral Programme)
grants.agency: CSIR (Council of Scientific and Industrial Research)
grants.description: Collaborative research between Indian CSIR labs and NIH/US institutions. Focus areas: infectious disease, genomics, computational biology.
grants.eligibility: CSIR laboratories; US NIH collaboration required
grants.brief: FUNDER PRIORITIES: The CSIR-NIH Bilateral Programme funds applied bilateral research in infectious disease surveillance, genomics, structural biology, and computational biology where Indian and US labs co-develop tools or datasets. CSIR rewards proposals that demonstrate translational value, shared infrastructure use (sequencing cores, biorepositories), and a clear publication or IP pipeline. Awards historically favour CSIR labs themselves (CCMB, IGIB, IMTECH), but university partners with computational or biosensing strength are increasingly added as nodes. CLIENT FIT: Ahmedabad University's verified strengths in advanced biosensing and bioanalysis techniques, nanoparticle synthesis, and computational/ML capacity make it a credible sub-awardee on a genomics or pathogen-detection node. The undergraduate research programme can supply trained student labour for sample preparation, sequencing QC, and pipeline development — a value-add CSIR PIs often lack. Past DST/SERB acknowledgements signal the institution clears central-government compliance hurdles. KEY REQUIREMENTS: (1) A CSIR laboratory must be the lead Indian applicant — Ahmedabad University must enter as a partnering institution, not PI. (2) A confirmed NIH-funded US co-investigator with an active R01 or U01 in scope. (3) Demonstrated biosafety, IRB, and data-sharing capacity meeting both ICMR and NIH protocols. STRATEGIC NOTE: Do not apply solo. Approach IGIB or CCMB faculty already collaborating with NIH on AMR or zoonotic surveillance and pitch a biosensing/ML sub-component leveraging the chemistry and CS faculty. Preliminary data needed: a working biosensor prototype or a published ML pipeline on public pathogen datasets. Calls are rolling — open conversations now and aim for a Q3 2026 submission window.

grants.strategy_memo:
THE OPPORTUNITY

This programme funds high-impact bilateral work in genomics, infectious disease, and computational biology with US NIH partners — areas where Indian institutions are systematically under-represented in NIH-linked funding. With your biosensing, nanomaterials, and computational biology strengths plus existing US/UK collaborations, you have a real shot at being pulled into a network project. But read the eligibility line carefully: this scheme is structured around CSIR laboratories as the lead Indian recipient, and Ahmedabad University is not a CSIR lab. Your path in is as a university partner inside a CSIR-led consortium, not as the prime applicant.

YOUR STRONGEST ANGLE

Lead with biosensing and computational biology applied to infectious disease surveillance in Gujarat and South Asia. That sits squarely inside the programme's three named focus areas, plays to your verified strengths in advanced biosensing/bioanalysis and nanoparticle synthesis, and gives a CSIR partner (IGIB, CCMB, or CDRI) something a national lab cannot easily supply on its own: regional clinical samples, an undergraduate research pipeline that generates throughput, and an established UK/US collaboration footprint. Frame Ahmedabad University as the translational and field arm — CSIR brings the genomics and regulatory infrastructure, NIH brings the comparative cohorts, you bring deployment in a real Indian disease-surveillance context.

THREE CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS

1. A confirmed CSIR lab co-lead in writing before you draft anything. Without a CSIR PI you are not eligible — full stop. Target IGIB (genomics), CDRI (infectious disease), or CCMB.
2. A named NIH-side collaborator with an active R01 or intramural project in the matching disease area, not a vague letter of interest. The US component is the gating dependency.
3. Preliminary biosensing or computational-biology data on an infectious-disease target (TB, dengue, AMR, vector-borne) — your textile/catalysis nanomaterials work will not carry this proposal alone. You need at least one figure showing detection or analysis on a clinical or clinically-relevant sample.

NEXT 30 DAYS

1. Have the Dean of Research email Dr. Souvik Maiti (Director, CSIR-IGIB) and Dr. Radha Rangarajan (Director, CSIR-CDRI) this week proposing a joint network proposal anchored on biosensing for infectious disease.
2. Ask Vyom Sharma to mine NIH RePORTER for active R01s in dengue, TB, or AMR diagnostics with PIs who have prior India collaborations, and shortlist three to approach.
3. Assign one undergraduate cohort under a faculty lead to generate preliminary biosensor detection data on a clinical infectious-disease target within four weeks — this is the figure that anchors the proposal.

grants.title: Indo-Australian Biotechnology Fund
grants.brief: FUNDER PRIORITIES: BIRAC's Indo-Australian Biotechnology Fund supports bilateral applied biotech projects with translational potential — diagnostics, vaccines, agri-biotech, industrial biotech, and bioinformatics platforms. Selection favours teams with prototype-stage technology, a clear commercialisation pathway, and a matched Australian partner with complementary capability (often via the Australian DFAT/ACIAR ecosystem). BIRAC values industry co-funding or LoIs and demonstrable IP positioning. CLIENT FIT: Ahmedabad University's verified strengths in advanced biosensing and bioanalysis, nanoparticle synthesis, and nanomaterials in catalysis are directly fundable as point-of-care diagnostic platforms or biosensor-based environmental monitoring tools. The institution's existing UK/US collaboration record signals capacity to manage bilateral compliance, MTAs, and joint IP. The undergraduate research programme can absorb device-prototyping and assay-validation work cost-effectively. KEY REQUIREMENTS: (1) Indian lead applicant must be a recognised biotech research entity — private non-profit university status qualifies, but DSIR recognition strengthens the file. (2) A bound Australian academic or industry partner with co-funding commitment. (3) A defined product or platform deliverable, not pure discovery research — TRL 3 or above expected. STRATEGIC NOTE: Apply jointly with an Australian partner; solo Indian applications are not eligible. Approach Monash, UNSW, or CSIRO Health & Biosecurity teams working on biosensors or nanodiagnostics. Preliminary data needed: a working device prototype with sensitivity/specificity numbers on at least one analyte, plus an Australian LoI. Watch the BIRAC website and DBT calendar — calls typically open annually in Q1; build the partnership now to be ready when the next window opens.

The Indo-Australian Biotechnology Fund is a bilateral instrument that rewards Indian institutions partnering with Australian counterparts on translational biotech — a near-perfect fit for Ahmedabad University given its existing UK/US collaboration infrastructure and verified strengths in nanoparticle synthesis and biosensing. With BIRAC's mandate tilted toward industry-relevant biotechnology, your published track record in advanced biosensing and nanomaterial catalysis gives you a credible launch pad most universities cannot match. Move now: bilateral calls are typically thin-windowed and reward teams with pre-formed Australian partnerships.

YOUR STRONGEST ANGLE
Lead with a translational nanobiosensing or nano-enabled diagnostics narrative anchored on Vyom Sharma's nanoparticle synthesis work and the institution's biosensing publication base. BIRAC funds biotechnology with commercialisation potential, not curiosity-driven science — frame the proposal around a deployable diagnostic or environmental-health monitoring device relevant to both Indian public health (TB, vector-borne disease, water contamination) and Australian priorities (One Health, antimicrobial resistance, remote-community diagnostics). The interdisciplinary undergraduate research model becomes a capacity-building bonus, not the headline. Cosmology, textiles, and theoretical physics do not belong anywhere in this application.

First, secure a named Australian co-PI with biotech credentials before drafting — without an MoU or letter of intent from a CSIRO lab, Monash, UQ AIBN, or similar, the application is dead on arrival. Second, generate preliminary data: a working biosensor prototype, characterisation data, or a pilot clinical/field sample set under Sharma's group within 60 days; BIRAC reviewers expect TRL 3–4 minimum. Third, lock down eligibility documentation early — DSIR recognition status, institutional 12A/80G certificates, and prior DST/SERB grant closure reports must be assembled now, not at submission.

grants.title: DMS/NIGMS 2: Spatial, Multi-Host Petri Net Models for Zoonotic Disease Forecasting
grants.description:
Diseases that spillover from wild animals pose an increasing threat to human health worldwide, but
forecasting how zoonotic pathogens spread remains a major challenge. Zoonotic diseases are complex,
spatially and temporally evolving systems whose behaviors are influenced by social, ecological, genetic,
and evolutionary factors. Understanding the contributions of biotic and abiotic factors to accurate disease forecasting is an urgent priority for managing the emerging risks of rapid environmental
grants.brief: FUNDER PRIORITIES: This DMS/NIGMS mathematical-biology track funds spatial stochastic models, Petri-net and agent-based frameworks, and multi-host disease dynamics with explicit ecological and evolutionary coupling. NIH wants methodological novelty (not just application), validated forecasts against real outbreak data, and open-source code. India-specific R01 award history (3 grants, ~$120K/year average) confirms NIH does fund Indian sub-awardees on zoonotic and One Health themes. CLIENT FIT: Ahmedabad University's combined capacity in machine learning, computational biology, and earth/environmental sciences maps cleanly onto spatial covariate modelling (land-use, climate layers) and ML-based disease forecasting. South Asian zoonotic hotspots (Nipah, Kyasanur, scrub typhus) give a US PI a compelling reason to add an Indian site. The interdisciplinary undergraduate programme can deliver data-curation and visualisation outputs that strengthen the broader-impacts section. KEY REQUIREMENTS: (1) US institution must be lead applicant; foreign component requires explicit scientific justification under NIH foreign-component rules. (2) Access to or generation of spatially resolved zoonotic surveillance data. (3) Mathematical/statistical methodology section meeting NIGMS rigour bar — Petri net or comparable formalism expected. STRATEGIC NOTE: Apply only as a foreign sub-award. Identify a US PI in mathematical epidemiology (NC State, Emory, Johns Hopkins) and offer Gujarat livestock-interface data plus ML modelling capacity. Preliminary data needed: a pilot spatial dataset and one preprint demonstrating forecasting methodology. Submission cycles are February/June/October — target the October 2026 round to allow data-sharing agreements and IRB to clear.

grants.brief: FUNDER PRIORITIES: NIEHS-led R25 SREEH funds structured summer research experiences for undergraduates in environmental health sciences — exposure science, environmental epidemiology, toxicology, and environmental data science. The mechanism rewards mentor depth, diversity recruitment, structured curriculum (responsible-conduct training, statistics, scientific communication), and measurable trainee outcomes (publications, graduate-school placement). NIH does not pay overhead-heavy international research; instead it funds trainee mobility and joint mentorship. CLIENT FIT: Ahmedabad University is uniquely positioned because its entire raison d'être is undergraduate research — exactly the population R25 SREEH serves. Strengths in environmental monitoring, earth sciences, sustainability, and data science offer US partners a low-cost, high-impact international placement site with real exposure data (air quality, water, climate) from Gujarat. STEM-education-India keyword and prior Ministry of Earth Sciences funding strengthen the case. KEY REQUIREMENTS: (1) US institution must be the lead applicant; foreign sites participate as training locations. (2) Structured mentorship plan with named mentors, learning objectives, and assessment rubrics. (3) Documented commitment to recruiting under-represented students and a clear evaluation framework. STRATEGIC NOTE: Do not lead — partner. Approach US universities with NIEHS-funded environmental-health centres (Columbia, Emory, Michigan, Harvard Chan) and propose Ahmedabad University as an international placement site offering authentic field exposure-science projects. Preliminary data needed: an MOU template, sample mentor CVs, and a curriculum outline. R25 receipt dates are typically May and September — target September 2026 for an FY27 start.

grants.brief: FUNDER PRIORITIES: NIH's Superfund Research Program (SRP) Training Cores fund integrated training pipelines tying environmental contaminant research to community engagement, with NIEHS prioritizing predoctoral/postdoctoral pipelines, hazardous substance toxicology, and translational community-facing outputs. CLIENT FIT: Ahmedabad University's strengths in advanced nanomaterials, biosensing/bioanalysis, and public health/epidemiology map onto contamination detection and exposure science, but this specific FOA is institutionally bound to Brown's Rhode Island ecosystem. The client's interdisciplinary undergraduate research model is conceptually aligned with SRP's training ethos but cannot serve as the core applicant. KEY REQUIREMENTS: (1) US-based lead institution holding an active SRP P42 center grant — Ahmedabad University cannot lead; (2) Predoctoral/postdoctoral trainee pipeline (excludes pure undergraduate models); (3) Demonstrated environmental health and community engagement infrastructure tied to the parent SRP. STRATEGIC NOTE: Do not apply solo — this is structurally infeasible. Pursue instead as a sub-recipient or international collaborator on a US SRP center's renewal (Brown, Boston University, Columbia, UNC), offering biosensing platforms or nanomaterial-based contaminant detection as complementary capability. Build preliminary data on Gujarat-relevant pollutants (industrial textile effluents, groundwater contaminants) and approach US SRP PIs 12–18 months ahead of their renewal cycle. A more direct domestic parallel is DST-SERB's Environmental Health cluster or DBT-NIH joint calls, which are better entry points.
